# Ray-Splat Intersection Algorithms

Also called: Ray-Gaussian Intersection, Ray Tracing for 3DGS, QuadBox, Plücker-based Splatting

## Overview
Ray-splat intersection algorithms evaluate the contribution of 3D Gaussians by intersecting viewing rays with the Gaussian primitives directly, rather than projecting them onto the image plane. This family solves the perspective distortion and depth-sorting artifacts inherent in tile-based rasterization [S1]. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) which approximates the projection as an affine 2D Gaussian, these methods provide exact or analytically derived intersections, enabling correct handling of semi-transparency and degenerate splats [S1].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family share the goal of computing the Gaussian's contribution $E$ along a ray $\mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}$. The core mathematical operation is finding the point $t_i$ along the ray where the Gaussian's density is maximized, often referred to as the "ray-Gaussian intersection" [S1]. This point is analytically derived from the Gaussian's covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, center $\mathbf{p}$, and the ray direction $\mathbf{v}$ (or $\mathbf{d}$) [S1]:

$$ t_i = \frac{\mathbf{v}^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} \mathbf{p}}{\mathbf{v}^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} \mathbf{v}} $$

The contribution is then modeled as a 1D Gaussian function along the ray:
$$ \rho(t) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(t - t_i)^2 k_i\right) $$
where $k_i$ is a curvature term derived from the covariance and ray direction [S1]. This reduces the 3D influence to a 1D function, allowing for exact integration or sampling [S1].

## Subtopics

### [Perspective-Correct 3D Gaussian Splatting via Plücker Coordinates](4556-perspective-correct-3d-gaussian-splatting-via-pl-cker-coordi.md)
This method provides a differentiable, matrix-inversion-free evaluation of 3D Gaussian densities along per-pixel viewing rays. It sets itself apart by extending Weyrich et al.'s 2D splatting techniques to 3D using Plücker coordinates, ensuring numerical stability even for degenerate splats where principal axes vanish. It eliminates the need for special handling of degenerate cases and avoids the numerical instabilities associated with matrix inversions in alternative rasterization-based approaches. Choose this when perspective correctness is critical and degenerate Gaussians are common.

### [Gaussian Opacity Fields (GOF)](5992-gaussian-opacity-fields-gof.md)
GOF replaces standard 2D projection rasterization with ray-tracing-based volume rendering. It analytically evaluates the maximum Gaussian contribution along each pixel ray, providing accurate depth estimation and facilitating the derivation of level-set surfaces from accumulated opacity. Unlike 3DGS, it does not rely on 2D projection integrals. Choose this when accurate depth and normal extraction are required alongside color rendering.

### [3D Gaussian Ray Tracing](8101-3d-gaussian-ray-tracing.md)
This method evaluates 3D Gaussian splats using hardware-accelerated ray tracing instead of rasterization. It solves the problem of linear scaling in dense scenes by using a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) to traverse only Gaussians that intersect the viewing ray, enabling logarithmic complexity relative to the number of splats. Unlike rasterization-based splatting which evaluates all Gaussians overlapping a tile, 3DGRT explicitly handles semi-transparency by accumulating transmittance through all intersected Gaussians, avoiding the depth-sorting artifacts inherent in tile-based rasterization. Choose this for large-scale scenes or when hardware ray tracing is available.

### [QuadBox](9231-quadbox.md)
QuadBox is a Gaussian-tile intersection method that uses four axis-aligned bounding boxes (AABBs) to tightly encapsulate projected 2D Gaussians. It sets itself apart by replacing the single conservative AABB with four symmetrically positioned, adaptively stretched sub-boxes that better fit the anisotropic shape of the ellipse. This tight fit suppresses empty tile coverage along the minor axis, while the accompanying QPass algorithm ensures deterministic, cache-friendly tile traversal with minimal per-tile overhead. Choose this when rasterization performance is prioritized but over-approximation of anisotropic splats is a bottleneck.

### Ray-Gaussian Intersection
This is the fundamental geometric operation shared by ray-based methods. It involves projecting the 3D Gaussian's covariance and center onto the camera ray to convert the 3D influence into a 1D Gaussian function along that specific ray [S1]. This allows for the analytical computation of the intersection point $t_i$ and the subsequent evaluation of the Gaussian's density along the ray [S1].

## Background
The concept of ray-Gaussian intersection originates from the need to accurately render 3D Gaussians without the approximations of affine projection. The analytical derivation of the intersection point $t_i$ is based on finding the extremum of the Gaussian function along a line, a technique detailed in "Approximate Differentiable Rendering with Algebraic Surfaces" [S1]. The specific formulation $\rho(t) = \exp(-\frac{1}{2}(t-t_i)^2 k_i)$ is used to map 3D Gaussian influence to 1D ray space [S1].
